title: Single-eigenstate test of eigenstate thermalization hypothesis via perturbed eigenstate quench
abstract: We propose and numerically validate an efficient single-eigenstate diagnostic for the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) based on a perturbed eigenstate quench protocol. By introducing a weak random perturbation to an energy eigenstate to break its stationarity, we characterize the time-averaged subsystem evolution speed as a function of the subsystem-to-total system size ratio. The diagnostic relies on a robust qualitative distinction: eigenstates satisfying ETH exhibit an S-shaped curve with a clear inflection point near half the system size, while ETH-violating eigenstates display a convex J-shaped profile. We benchmark the criterion across paradigmatic one-dimensional spin chains covering chaotic, integrable, many-body localized, and quantum many-body scar regimes, obtaining full agreement with established thermalization phenomenology. Our method circumvents the need for explicit thermal ensemble construction, providing a robust, experimentally feasible probe of eigenstate thermalization at the single-eigenstate level.
summary: The authors propose a novel diagnostic using a perturbed eigenstate quench to test the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) at the level of individual energy eigenstates. By analyzing the time-averaged subsystem evolution speed versus system size ratio, they distinguish ETH-obeying states (S-shaped curve) from non-thermalizing ones (J-shaped curve). This method is robustly tested across diverse 1D spin chain models.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop an efficient, single-eigenstate diagnostic tool to test the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) in isolated quantum many-body systems.
main_result: A novel quench protocol distinguishes ETH-obeying eigenstates, which show an S-shaped curve with an inflection point at half system size, from ETH-violating states, which exhibit a convex J-shape.
method: The diagnostic uses a 'perturbed eigenstate quench' protocol, evolving a weakly perturbed initial state $|\psi(0)angle$ under the original Hamiltonian and measuring the time-averaged subsystem evolution speed $\langle v_A(t) angle$.
model_or_system: The method is benchmarked across various 1D spin chains, including chaotic/integrable Ising models, disordered XXZ chains (covering ergodic to MBL regimes), and a spin-1 XX chain exhibiting scar states.
key_observables: Time-averaged subsystem evolution speed $\langle v_A(t) angle$ plotted against the subsystem size ratio $x = \ell/L$.
important_parameters: The perturbation strength ($\epsilon=10^{-3}$), and the system parameters defining different quantum regimes (e.g., disorder strength in XXZ chains).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the time-averaged speed $\langle v_A(t) angle$ provides a robust, qualitative distinction between thermalizing and non-thermalizing dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures compare the normalized evolution speed versus subsystem size ratio for different eigenstates (e.g., ground state vs. bulk states) across various Hamiltonian regimes.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of single-eigenstate ETH testing, details the perturbed eigenstate quench methodology, presents the characteristic S-shaped vs. J-shaped signatures, and validates this diagnostic across multiple paradigmatic 1D spin chain models.
why_interesting: This provides a powerful, computationally feasible probe for understanding thermalization dynamics in isolated quantum systems without needing to construct full thermal ensembles, which is highly relevant for AMO platforms simulating many-body physics.
